Phileas Fogg and Aouda went on board, where they found Fix already installed. Below deck was a square cabin, of which the walls bulged out in the form of cots, above a circular divan; in the centre was a table provided with a swinging lamp. The accommodation was confined, but neat.
“I am sorry to have nothing better to offer you,” said Mr. Fogg to Fix, who bowed without responding.
The detective had a feeling akin to humiliation in profiting by the kindness of Mr. Fogg.
“It’s certain,” thought he, “though rascal as he is, he is a polite one!”

The sails and the English flag were hoisted at ten minutes past three. Mr. Fogg and Aouda, who were seated on deck, cast a last glance at the quay, in the hope of espying Passepartout. Fix was not without his fears lest chance should direct the steps of the unfortunate servant, whom he had so badly treated, in this direction; in which case an explanation the reverse of satisfactory to the detective must have ensued. But the Frenchman did not appear, and, without doubt, was still lying under the stupefying influence of the opium.
John Bunsby, master, at length gave the order to start, and the “Tankadere,” taking the wind under her brigantine, foresail, and standing-jib, bounded briskly forward over the waves.
translated_paragraphs: 鸦片馆里发生这些事的时候，福克先生并不知道自己眼看要误船，仍安安稳稳地陪着艾娥达走在英国人居住的街区，购买后面那趟漫长航程所需的物品。像福克先生这样的英国人，拎一只旅行袋就可以环游世界；可要一位女士靠这么一点行装，舒舒服服走完全程，就不能理所当然了。他办这件差事，仍然显出那副特有的沉静。他的女伴一再为他的耐心与慷慨感到过意不去，他的回答也始终如一：
“这是为了我的行程好。它是我计划的一部分。”
采购停当，他们回到旅馆，在丰盛而讲究的公共餐桌上用过晚饭。随后，艾娥达照英国习惯跟她的保护人握了握手，回房休息。福克先生整个晚上都埋头于《泰晤士报》和《伦敦新闻画报》。
世上若真有什么能叫他吃惊的事，上床时仆人竟还没回来，大概算得上一件。可他只知道去横滨的轮船要明早才开，于是并没为此费心。次日清晨，主人按铃，万事通没有应声露面。福克先生丝毫不显懊恼，只是拿起旅行袋，叫上艾娥达，吩咐人去雇一顶轿子。
那时是八点钟。九点半涨潮，“卡尔纳蒂克号”就要出港。福克和艾娥达坐进轿里，行李在后面用独轮小车推着。半个钟头后，他们踏上准备登船的码头。这时福克才得知，“卡尔纳蒂克号”昨晚已经开走。他本来以为船和仆人都在这里等着他，如今两个都不可得。脸上却不见一丝失望。他只是对艾娥达说：“太太，这是个意外罢了，仅此而已。”
这时，一个先前一直仔细打量他的人走上前来，原来是菲克斯。他鞠躬向福克招呼道：“先生，您同我一样，是昨天到港的‘仰光号’上的旅客，对吗？”
“是的，先生，”福克淡淡地答道，“不过，我还没有荣幸——”
“请原谅，我原以为会在这儿见到您的仆人。”
“先生，您知道他在哪里吗？”艾娥达焦急地问。
“怎么！”菲克斯装出吃惊的神色，“他难道没有跟两位在一起？”
“没有，”艾娥达说，“昨天以来，他一直没有再露面。他会不会没等我们，自己上了‘卡尔纳蒂克号’？”
“没等你们，太太？”警探答道，“恕我冒昧，两位原定是乘‘卡尔纳蒂克号’启程吗？”
“是的，先生。”
“太太，我也是。可我实在失望透了。‘卡尔纳蒂克号’的修理完工，没另行通知，竟比预定时刻早十二小时离开了香港。现在要等下一艘轮船，我们得等足一个星期。”
说出“一个星期”几个字，菲克斯高兴得心都猛跳了一下。福克给困在香港一个星期！这下逮捕令来得及送到，运气到底还是眷顾了他这个执法的人。可想而知，听见福克用那副平平静静的嗓音说出下一句话时，他心里有多么骇然：“不过，依我看，香港港内可不光是‘卡尔纳蒂克号’一艘船。”
说完，福克向艾娥达伸出臂膀，转身迈向各处码头，寻找一艘准备启航的船。目瞪口呆的菲克斯跟在后面，仿佛有根看不见的细线把他系在了福克身上。然而，这一回，先前那样肯帮福克的机缘似乎真要弃他而去了。他沿码头寻找了整整三个钟头，打定主意，若有必要，就包一艘船送他去横滨。可他找到的船，不是正装货，就是在卸货，没有一艘能马上出航。菲克斯心里又燃起了希望。
可是福克先生远未灰心，仍继续寻找，哪怕得到澳门去找也不肯罢手。就在一个码头上，有个水手上前跟他搭话。
“老爷是在找船吗？”
“你有一艘准备好随时开航的船吗？”
“有，老爷。一艘引水船，四十三号，全港最好的船。”
“走得快吗？”
“八节到九节之间。您想看看船吗？”
“老爷一定会满意的。是想出海游玩一番？”
“不，是要航行去别处。”
“航行？”
“对。你愿意送我去横滨吗？”
水手靠在栏杆上，眼睛睁得很大：“老爷在说笑吧？”
“不。我错过了‘卡尔纳蒂克号’，最迟十四日必须到横滨，搭去旧金山的轮船。”
“很遗憾，”水手说，“这做不到。”
“我出每天一百英镑。如果我能按时到达横滨，再给你两百英镑的酬金。”
“您是说真的吗？”
“句句当真。”
引水员走开几步，眺望大海，显然是在挣扎：一面想挣到一大笔钱，一面又害怕冒险远航。菲克斯在一旁等着结果，心悬得快落不下来了。
福克先生转向艾娥达，问她：“太太，你不会害怕吧？”
“只要有您同行，福克先生，我就不怕。”她答道。
引水员回来了，双手不停地翻弄他的帽子。
“怎么样，引水员？”福克先生问。
“老爷，这么说吧，”他答道，“一年当中的这个季节，我不能拿自己、几个伙计，以及这条还不到二十吨的小船去走这样的长途，冒这个险。再说，也赶不到横滨，因为那里离香港有一千六百六十英里。”
“只有一千六百英里。”福克先生说。
“那也差不离。”
菲克斯透过了一口气。
“不过，”引水员接着说，“倒是可以有另一种安排。”
菲克斯立刻连气都透不过了。
“什么办法？”福克问。
“去日本最南端的长崎，或者干脆去上海。上海离这儿不过八百英里。去上海不必驶离中国海岸太远，这一点大为有利：沿岸海流向北，能帮我们一把。”
“引水员，我得在横滨搭上那艘美国轮船，”福克说，“不是到上海或长崎搭。”
“为什么不能呢？”引水员反问，“开往旧金山的轮船可不是从横滨发船的。它停靠横滨和长崎，起点却是上海。”
“你拿得准吗？”
“完全拿得准。”
“轮船什么时候离开上海？”
“十一日晚上七点。所以，我们有四天的工夫，也就是九十六个小时。这段时间，若运气好，吹西南风，海面又平静，我们可以走完到上海的八百英里。”
“那你什么时候能动身——”
“一个小时后。只要把粮食装上船，把帆张起来就成。”
“成交。你是这条船的船长？”
“是的。约翰·邦斯比，‘坦卡代尔号’船长。”
“需要先付一笔定金吗？”
“只要不给老爷添麻烦——”
“这里是预付的两百英镑。”菲利亚斯·福克又转向菲克斯，“先生，你要是愿意利用这个机会——”
“多谢，先生。我正要开口叨这份光呢。”
“很好。半个钟头以后，我们上船。”
“可怜的万事通呢？”艾娥达追问。仆人失踪了，她一直非常担心。
“我会尽我所能去找他。”菲利亚斯·福克答道。
菲克斯在紧张不安中走向引水船，另外两人则前往香港警署。福克先生在那里留下万事通的相貌描述，又留下一笔钱给他们用来找人。他们随后到法国领事馆，照样把这两件事办了一遍。轿子还在旅馆门口停下，取了先前送回去的行李，他们才重返码头。
这时是三点。四十三号引水船的船员已全数到齐，给养也装好，只等启航。

“坦卡代尔号”是条利落的小船，二十吨左右，线条优美，像为竞速而建的游艇。明亮的铜皮船壳、镀锌的铁件、白得像象牙的甲板，都看得出约翰·邦斯比多么以打扮自己的船为荣。两根桅杆稍向后斜，配有后桅纵帆、前帆、风暴前支索帆和常用的前支索帆，整套帆装极适合顺风航行。看模样就知它快得很；实际上，它早在引水船比赛中赢过好几回奖，已证明了这份本领。“坦卡代尔号”的人手，除船长约翰·邦斯比以外，还有四名熟悉中国海域的健壮水手。邦斯比本人四十五岁上下，精力充沛，皮肤晒成古铜色，眼神有活力，脸上有魄力，也有自信。就是最胆小的人，见他也能放心。
菲利亚斯·福克和艾娥达登上船时，菲克斯已安顿妥当。甲板以下是一方小舱，环舱有一圈长榻，长榻上方，舱壁向外凸出，形成卧铺。正中一张桌子，配着一盏能随船摇摆而保持平稳的灯。地方不宽敞，倒是整整洁洁。
“没能给你安排更好的住处，很遗憾。”福克先生对菲克斯说。后者鞠了一躬，没有回答。
承受着福克先生这份好意，警探心里甚至有些近乎屈辱的滋味。
“有一点很清楚，”他想，“这家伙就算是个贼，也是个有礼貌的贼！”
三点十分，船帆和英国国旗同时升起。福克和艾娥达坐在甲板上，最后朝码头望了一眼，希望还能瞥见万事通。菲克斯也不免有些害怕，万一机缘把那名受了他如此亏待的仆人碰巧引到这里，他少不得要作一番解释，那情形对于警探可绝不称心。可是法国人没有出现，想必此刻仍然伏卧在鸦片的麻醉之中。
船长约翰·邦斯比终于下令开船。“坦卡代尔号”的后桅纵帆、前帆和前支索帆吃满了风，轻快地跃过浪头，向前驶去。

sections.title_zh: 第21章　“坦卡代尔号”的船长很有可能失去两百英镑酬金
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XXI. — IN WHICH THE MASTER OF THE “TANKADERE” RUNS GREAT RISK OF LOSING A REWARD OF TWO HUNDRED POUNDS
source_paragraphs: This voyage of eight hundred miles was a perilous venture on a craft of twenty tons, and at that season of the year. The Chinese seas are usually boisterous, subject to terrible gales of wind, and especially during the equinoxes; and it was now early November.

It would clearly have been to the master’s advantage to carry his passengers to Yokohama, since he was paid a certain sum per day; but he would have been rash to attempt such a voyage, and it was imprudent even to attempt to reach Shanghai. But John Bunsby believed in the “Tankadere,” which rode on the waves like a seagull; and perhaps he was not wrong.
Late in the day they passed through the capricious channels of Hong Kong, and the “Tankadere,” impelled by favourable winds, conducted herself admirably.
“I do not need, pilot,” said Phileas Fogg, when they got into the open sea, “to advise you to use all possible speed.”
“Trust me, your honour. We are carrying all the sail the wind will let us. The poles would add nothing, and are only used when we are going into port.”
“It’s your trade, not mine, pilot, and I confide in you.”

Phileas Fogg, with body erect and legs wide apart, standing like a sailor, gazed without staggering at the swelling waters. The young woman, who was seated aft, was profoundly affected as she looked out upon the ocean, darkening now with the twilight, on which she had ventured in so frail a vessel. Above her head rustled the white sails, which seemed like great white wings. The boat, carried forward by the wind, seemed to be flying in the air.

Night came. The moon was entering her first quarter, and her insufficient light would soon die out in the mist on the horizon. Clouds were rising from the east, and already overcast a part of the heavens.

The pilot had hung out his lights, which was very necessary in these seas crowded with vessels bound landward; for collisions are not uncommon occurrences, and, at the speed she was going, the least shock would shatter the gallant little craft.

Fix, seated in the bow, gave himself up to meditation. He kept apart from his fellow-travellers, knowing Mr. Fogg’s taciturn tastes; besides, he did not quite like to talk to the man whose favours he had accepted. He was thinking, too, of the future. It seemed certain that Fogg would not stop at Yokohama, but would at once take the boat for San Francisco; and the vast extent of America would ensure him impunity and safety. Fogg’s plan appeared to him the simplest in the world. Instead of sailing directly from England to the United States, like a common villain, he had traversed three quarters of the globe, so as to gain the American continent more surely; and there, after throwing the police off his track, he would quietly enjoy himself with the fortune stolen from the bank. But, once in the United States, what should he, Fix, do? Should he abandon this man? No, a hundred times no! Until he had secured his extradition, he would not lose sight of him for an hour. It was his duty, and he would fulfil it to the end. At all events, there was one thing to be thankful for; Passepartout was not with his master; and it was above all important, after the confidences Fix had imparted to him, that the servant should never have speech with his master.

Phileas Fogg was also thinking of Passepartout, who had so strangely disappeared. Looking at the matter from every point of view, it did not seem to him impossible that, by some mistake, the man might have embarked on the “Carnatic” at the last moment; and this was also Aouda’s opinion, who regretted very much the loss of the worthy fellow to whom she owed so much. They might then find him at Yokohama; for, if the “Carnatic” was carrying him thither, it would be easy to ascertain if he had been on board.

A brisk breeze arose about ten o’clock; but, though it might have been prudent to take in a reef, the pilot, after carefully examining the heavens, let the craft remain rigged as before. The “Tankadere” bore sail admirably, as she drew a great deal of water, and everything was prepared for high speed in case of a gale.
Mr. Fogg and Aouda descended into the cabin at midnight, having been already preceded by Fix, who had lain down on one of the cots. The pilot and crew remained on deck all night.

At sunrise the next day, which was 8th November, the boat had made more than one hundred miles. The log indicated a mean speed of between eight and nine miles. The “Tankadere” still carried all sail, and was accomplishing her greatest capacity of speed. If the wind held as it was, the chances would be in her favour. During the day she kept along the coast, where the currents were favourable; the coast, irregular in profile, and visible sometimes across the clearings, was at most five miles distant. The sea was less boisterous, since the wind came off land—a fortunate circumstance for the boat, which would suffer, owing to its small tonnage, by a heavy surge on the sea.
The breeze subsided a little towards noon, and set in from the south-west. The pilot put up his poles, but took them down again within two hours, as the wind freshened up anew.

Mr. Fogg and Aouda, happily unaffected by the roughness of the sea, ate with a good appetite, Fix being invited to share their repast, which he accepted with secret chagrin. To travel at this man’s expense and live upon his provisions was not palatable to him. Still, he was obliged to eat, and so he ate.

When the meal was over, he took Mr. Fogg apart, and said, “sir”—this “sir” scorched his lips, and he had to control himself to avoid collaring this “gentleman”—“sir, you have been very kind to give me a passage on this boat. But, though my means will not admit of my expending them as freely as you, I must ask to pay my share—”
“Let us not speak of that, sir,” replied Mr. Fogg.
“But, if I insist—”
“No, sir,” repeated Mr. Fogg, in a tone which did not admit of a reply. “This enters into my general expenses.”
Fix, as he bowed, had a stifled feeling, and, going forward, where he ensconced himself, did not open his mouth for the rest of the day.

Meanwhile they were progressing famously, and John Bunsby was in high hope. He several times assured Mr. Fogg that they would reach Shanghai in time; to which that gentleman responded that he counted upon it. The crew set to work in good earnest, inspired by the reward to be gained. There was not a sheet which was not tightened, not a sail which was not vigorously hoisted; not a lurch could be charged to the man at the helm. They worked as desperately as if they were contesting in a Royal yacht regatta.

By evening, the log showed that two hundred and twenty miles had been accomplished from Hong Kong, and Mr. Fogg might hope that he would be able to reach Yokohama without recording any delay in his journal; in which case, the many misadventures which had overtaken him since he left London would not seriously affect his journey.

The “Tankadere” entered the Straits of Fo-Kien, which separate the island of Formosa from the Chinese coast, in the small hours of the night, and crossed the Tropic of Cancer. The sea was very rough in the straits, full of eddies formed by the counter-currents, and the chopping waves broke her course, whilst it became very difficult to stand on deck.

At daybreak the wind began to blow hard again, and the heavens seemed to predict a gale. The barometer announced a speedy change, the mercury rising and falling capriciously; the sea also, in the south-east, raised long surges which indicated a tempest. The sun had set the evening before in a red mist, in the midst of the phosphorescent scintillations of the ocean.
John Bunsby long examined the threatening aspect of the heavens, muttering indistinctly between his teeth. At last he said in a low voice to Mr. Fogg, “Shall I speak out to your honour?”
“Of course.”
“Well, we are going to have a squall.”
“Is the wind north or south?” asked Mr. Fogg quietly.
“South. Look! a typhoon is coming up.”
“Glad it’s a typhoon from the south, for it will carry us forward.”

“Oh, if you take it that way,” said John Bunsby, “I’ve nothing more to say.” John Bunsby’s suspicions were confirmed. At a less advanced season of the year the typhoon, according to a famous meteorologist, would have passed away like a luminous cascade of electric flame; but in the winter equinox it was to be feared that it would burst upon them with great violence.

The pilot took his precautions in advance. He reefed all sail, the pole-masts were dispensed with; all hands went forward to the bows. A single triangular sail, of strong canvas, was hoisted as a storm-jib, so as to hold the wind from behind. Then they waited.

John Bunsby had requested his passengers to go below; but this imprisonment in so narrow a space, with little air, and the boat bouncing in the gale, was far from pleasant. Neither Mr. Fogg, Fix, nor Aouda consented to leave the deck.

The storm of rain and wind descended upon them towards eight o’clock. With but its bit of sail, the “Tankadere” was lifted like a feather by a wind, an idea of whose violence can scarcely be given. To compare her speed to four times that of a locomotive going on full steam would be below the truth.

The boat scudded thus northward during the whole day, borne on by monstrous waves, preserving always, fortunately, a speed equal to theirs. Twenty times she seemed almost to be submerged by these mountains of water which rose behind her; but the adroit management of the pilot saved her. The passengers were often bathed in spray, but they submitted to it philosophically. Fix cursed it, no doubt; but Aouda, with her eyes fastened upon her protector, whose coolness amazed her, showed herself worthy of him, and bravely weathered the storm. As for Phileas Fogg, it seemed just as if the typhoon were a part of his programme.

Up to this time the “Tankadere” had always held her course to the north; but towards evening the wind, veering three quarters, bore down from the north-west. The boat, now lying in the trough of the waves, shook and rolled terribly; the sea struck her with fearful violence. At night the tempest increased in violence. John Bunsby saw the approach of darkness and the rising of the storm with dark misgivings. He thought awhile, and then asked his crew if it was not time to slacken speed. After a consultation he approached Mr. Fogg, and said, “I think, your honour, that we should do well to make for one of the ports on the coast.”
“I think so too.”
“Ah!” said the pilot. “But which one?”
“I know of but one,” returned Mr. Fogg tranquilly.
“And that is—”
“Shanghai.”
The pilot, at first, did not seem to comprehend; he could scarcely realise so much determination and tenacity. Then he cried, “Well—yes! Your honour is right. To Shanghai!”
So the “Tankadere” kept steadily on her northward track.

The night was really terrible; it would be a miracle if the craft did not founder. Twice it could have been all over with her if the crew had not been constantly on the watch. Aouda was exhausted, but did not utter a complaint. More than once Mr. Fogg rushed to protect her from the violence of the waves.

Day reappeared. The tempest still raged with undiminished fury; but the wind now returned to the south-east. It was a favourable change, and the “Tankadere” again bounded forward on this mountainous sea, though the waves crossed each other, and imparted shocks and counter-shocks which would have crushed a craft less solidly built. From time to time the coast was visible through the broken mist, but no vessel was in sight. The “Tankadere” was alone upon the sea.

There were some signs of a calm at noon, and these became more distinct as the sun descended toward the horizon. The tempest had been as brief as terrific. The passengers, thoroughly exhausted, could now eat a little, and take some repose.

The night was comparatively quiet. Some of the sails were again hoisted, and the speed of the boat was very good. The next morning at dawn they espied the coast, and John Bunsby was able to assert that they were not one hundred miles from Shanghai. A hundred miles, and only one day to traverse them! That very evening Mr. Fogg was due at Shanghai, if he did not wish to miss the steamer to Yokohama. Had there been no storm, during which several hours were lost, they would be at this moment within thirty miles of their destination.

The wind grew decidedly calmer, and happily the sea fell with it. All sails were now hoisted, and at noon the “Tankadere” was within forty-five miles of Shanghai. There remained yet six hours in which to accomplish that distance. All on board feared that it could not be done, and every one—Phileas Fogg, no doubt, excepted—felt his heart beat with impatience. The boat must keep up an average of nine miles an hour, and the wind was becoming calmer every moment! It was a capricious breeze, coming from the coast, and after it passed the sea became smooth. Still, the “Tankadere” was so light, and her fine sails caught the fickle zephyrs so well, that, with the aid of the currents John Bunsby found himself at six o’clock not more than ten miles from the mouth of Shanghai River. Shanghai itself is situated at least twelve miles up the stream. At seven they were still three miles from Shanghai. The pilot swore an angry oath; the reward of two hundred pounds was evidently on the point of escaping him. He looked at Mr. Fogg. Mr. Fogg was perfectly tranquil; and yet his whole fortune was at this moment at stake.
At this moment, also, a long black funnel, crowned with wreaths of smoke, appeared on the edge of the waters. It was the American steamer, leaving for Yokohama at the appointed time.
“Confound her!” cried John Bunsby, pushing back the rudder with a desperate jerk.
“Signal her!” said Phileas Fogg quietly.

A small brass cannon stood on the forward deck of the “Tankadere,” for making signals in the fogs. It was loaded to the muzzle; but just as the pilot was about to apply a red-hot coal to the touchhole, Mr. Fogg said, “Hoist your flag!”
The flag was run up at half-mast, and, this being the signal of distress, it was hoped that the American steamer, perceiving it, would change her course a little, so as to succour the pilot-boat.
“Fire!” said Mr. Fogg. And the booming of the little cannon resounded in the air.
translated_paragraphs: 在这般时节，乘一艘二十吨的小帆船走八百英里的海路，实在是在冒险。中国近海向来多风浪，有时会起可怕的暴风，春秋昼夜平分前后尤其如此。眼下，已经到了十一月初。
邦斯比若将旅客一直送到横滨，论每天计酬的办法，显然对他更为有利。可是试图走那么远，那就太莽撞；其实，只求到上海也已算不得谨慎。约翰·邦斯比却相信“坦卡代尔号”。它在浪尖上起伏，轻巧得像一只海鸥。说不定，他有道理。
这天稍晚，小船穿过香港那些曲折难测的水道。“坦卡代尔号”借着顺风，大大显了一番身手。
“引水员，”进入外海以后，菲利亚斯·福克说，“用不着我提醒你，要尽可能开快一些。”
“老爷尽管放心。风力允许用多少帆，我们就用了多少。再张撑杆也添不了速度，一般只有进港时我们才用它们。”
“引水员，行船是你的本行，并不是我的。我相信你。”
菲利亚斯·福克身躯挺直，两脚分开，像个水手般牢牢站定，一动不晃地望着翻涌的海面。年轻女子坐在船尾，看着这海洋在暮色中渐渐发黑，想到自己竟乘这样单薄的小船闯到这里，心头大受触动。白帆在她头顶沙沙作响，看上去恍若巨大的白翅膀。船给风托着往前，几乎像是飞在半空。
入夜了。月亮正进上弦，那微弱的一线月光不久就会在地平线的雾气中熄灭。东面升起云团，已经遮住了一角天。
引水员挂起了灯。这里驶向陆地的船只密集，船灯十分要紧，因为碰撞并非罕见。而以眼下的船速，哪怕轻轻擦一下，也足以叫这艘勇敢的小船粉身碎骨。

菲克斯坐在船首，陷入沉思。他知道福克先生不爱说话，就同两位旅伴保持一点距离。何况他受了这人的好处，自己也不大乐意跟他交谈。他还在想以后的事。看起来几乎可以确定，福克到了横滨并不停留，会立刻搭上旧金山的船。美国地方辽阔，足以让他安全藏匿，免受惩罚。福克所打的算盘，依他看是世上最明白不过的了。普通的恶棍才会从英国直接坐船去美国；他却绕过四分之三个地球，好更有把握地抵达美洲大陆。到了那里，警察既已给他摆脱，便可安安稳稳享用从银行偷来的巨款。那么，等他到了美国，他菲克斯又该怎么办？放弃这个人？不，一百次不！在引渡手续办妥以前，连一个钟头也不能让他离开自己的视线。那是他的职责，他要执行到底。无论如何，倒有一件事值得庆幸：万事通现在没跟主人在一起。菲克斯已向仆人透露过秘密，最要紧的就是决不能叫他有机会跟主人说话。
菲利亚斯·福克也在想，那样莫名其妙失了踪的万事通到底去了哪里。他从各方面想过，并不能排除这个可能：万事通因某种误会，最后一刻已登上了“卡尔纳蒂克号”。艾娥达也这样想。那位老实伙伴帮过她那么多忙，如今不知去向，使她十分惋惜。若他已在船上，他们兴许能在横滨重逢。毕竟，只要“卡尔纳蒂克号”确曾搭他去那儿，要查明他是否在船上，并不难。
十点钟左右，风更劲了。谨慎些本该收起一缩帆，可引水员仔细打量天色之后，仍让所有的帆保持原样。“坦卡代尔号”吃水相当深，大帆在它身上很经得住风，什么都准备妥当，一旦起了强风，正可全速疾驶。
午夜，福克和艾娥达下了舱。菲克斯先他们一步，已经在一侧的铺上躺下。引水员和水手则整夜待在甲板上。
次日十一月八日日出时，小船已走过一百多英里。测程仪显示，平均时速在八到九英里之间。“坦卡代尔号”仍然张满全部风帆，船速已发挥到极致。只要风向不改，他们便很有希望。白天，小船贴着海岸前进，沿岸海流是顺的。海岸线参差起伏，偶尔在天气开朗的空当里显出身影，最远也不过离船五英里。风从陆上吹来，海面便不那样汹涌。对于吨位这么小的船，这是幸事；若遇上外海的长涌，它可要吃些苦头。
近中午，风势稍歇，转从西南而来。引水员架起撑杆。还没过两个钟头，风又加劲，他便把撑杆撤了下来。
幸好福克和艾娥达都没受海浪颠簸的影响，吃起东西来很有胃口。他们邀菲克斯一同进餐，他内心懊恼，却还是接受了。搭这人的船，吃这人的粮，实在不合他的胃口；然而饭总不能不吃，他也就吃了。
饭后，他将福克请到一旁，说：“先生——”这个“先生”把他的嘴唇烫得生疼。他非得克制自己，才没一把揪住这位“绅士”的领子。“先生，承蒙你好意准我搭船。我的财力虽不像你，可以任意花费，可我必须请求支付自己那一份——”
“先生，这件事就不必说了。”福克先生答道。
“可是，如果我坚持——”
“不，先生，”福克先生又说了一遍，语气不容争辩，“这笔钱列入我的总开支。”
菲克斯鞠了一躬，胸口有种被堵住了的感觉。他走到船首，在那里找了个僻静角落，直到天黑再没有开口。
小船这一路进展十分顺利，约翰·邦斯比满怀希望。他好几次向福克保证，准能按时到达上海。福克总是答道，他正指望能如此。水手们想到快可赚着的那几笔酬劳，个个十分卖力。不论哪根帆脚索都拉得紧，不论哪面帆都鼓足了劲扯，船舵掌得稳，船身一回横摆也怪不到舵手头上。大家拼命的劲头，简直像在争夺皇家游艇赛的奖杯。
到了傍晚，测程仪显示，他们离香港已有二百二十英里。福克先生甚至很可以希望，到横滨时，他不用在日程表上记下任何误点。这样一来，离开伦敦以来遭遇的种种波折，就都不会严重影响行程了。
后半夜，“坦卡代尔号”驶入台湾岛与中国大陆之间的福建海峡，穿过了北回归线。海峡内波浪汹涌，相向的海流造成许多旋涡，短促杂乱的浪头不断冲击船身。连在甲板上站稳都变得非常困难。
天亮时，风又刮紧了。天色似在预告一场大风。气压计里的水银忽高忽低，预示着天气很快就要突变；东南方海面上，长浪也一道道隆起，是风暴将至的征兆。昨天下午，海面上磷光星星点点，太阳就在一片红雾中落了下去。
约翰·邦斯比久久观察那凶险的天色，牙缝里一直模糊地咕哝着什么。最后，他低声向福克问道：“老爷，许我直说吗？”
“当然。”
“好，我们就要遇上一阵暴风了。”
“是北风，还是南风？”福克先生平静地问。
“南风。您瞧！台风正要过来。”
“我很高兴，是从南面来的台风。它会把我们往前送。”
“哦，您要是这样看，”约翰·邦斯比说，“那我没别的话了。”邦斯比的疑虑很快得到证实。若是一年当中稍早的季节，按照一位著名气象学家的说法，这种台风会像一阵发光的电火瀑布一样掠过。可眼下已近冬季，它恐怕要凶猛无比地扑上来了。
引水员提前作了防备。他将所有船帆尽数缩起，撤掉上桅的细杆，叫全体水手赶到船头。只升起一小面坚牢帆布制的三角帆，充作风暴前帆，好兜住从后面刮来的风。随后，他们等待着。
邦斯比曾请旅客下舱。可要把自己禁闭在如此狭窄、空气稀薄的地方，还要随着小船在大风里抛上抛下，实在谈不上愉快。因此，福克先生、菲克斯和艾娥达没有一个肯离开甲板。
将近八点，狂风暴雨向他们迎头压下。那风有多凶猛，几乎没法叫人想象。“坦卡代尔号”只剩一小片船帆，也给它像羽毛一样托了起来。若说船速足有全速蒸汽火车的四倍，那还小看它了。
小船这样乘着骇人的巨浪，整整一天向北狂奔。幸好它总能使速度同浪头相当。背后竖起了山一样的海水，至少有二十次，它看上去几乎要给淹没，全靠引水员身手高明才逃过了。旅客们时常被浪花从头到脚浇透，倒还豁达地忍受着。菲克斯大概在心里痛骂就是了。艾娥达把双眼望定保护她的人，他的镇静叫她惊异，她自己也表现得配得上他，勇敢地抵挡风暴。至于福克，看上去仿佛这场台风本来就是他计划的一部分。
到此时，“坦卡代尔号”始终守着向北的航线。可近傍晚，风向一转好几个方位，改从西北压过来。小船落在浪谷里，剧烈地摇晃翻滚，海浪以可怕的力量撞击船身。入夜以后，风暴越发凶猛。约翰·邦斯比看着黑暗逼近、风势增强，心里疑虑重重。他考虑片刻，问水手们是不是该放慢船速了。商量过以后，他来到福克跟前说：“老爷，我想，我们最好找个沿海的港口开进去。”
“我也这么想。”
“啊！”引水员说，“可是去哪个港口呢？”
“我只知道一个。”福克先生安然答道。
“那就是——”
“上海。”
起初，引水员仿佛没听明白。他实在很难想象，一个人能有这样的决心，又能如此坚持。接着他喊道：“好吧——对！老爷说得对。去上海！”
于是“坦卡代尔号”坚定地守住航线，继续北上。
那真是可怕的一夜。这船要是不沉，已堪称奇迹。有两次，要不是船员时时处处警醒，整条船就都完了。艾娥达已经精疲力竭，却没发一句牢骚。好几回，福克先生都抢上前去，替她抵挡猛扑过来的海浪。
天又亮了。风暴仍毫不减劲地怒吼着，但风向如今转回了东南。这个变化于他们有利，“坦卡代尔号”又一次在群山一般的海面上飞跃前进。只是浪峰交错，一撞又跟着反向一撞。换一条造得不这样结实的船，早该粉碎了。沿岸轮廓不时从断裂的雾中出现，却看不见任何其他船舶。海面上只有“坦卡代尔号”孤零零的一条船。
中午，风浪略现平息的兆头；等太阳滑向地平线，这种兆头越发明显。风暴来得可怕，去得也快。旅客们彻底耗尽了力气，现在总算吃得下一点东西，也能稍事歇息。
夜里相当平静。船上又挂起几面帆，航速很好。次日拂晓，他们望见海岸，约翰·邦斯比已能断定，到上海不满一百英里。一百英里，只剩一天去走完它！福克先生要想搭上去横滨的轮船，就得在当夜赶到上海。要不是风暴耽误了几小时，他们此刻离目的地已不超过三十英里了。

风明显平息了，幸好，海面也跟着平静下来。全部风帆现已升起。中午，“坦卡代尔号”离上海不到四十五英里，还余六小时去走完这段路。全船的人都担心他们办不到。除了菲利亚斯·福克大概是个例外，其余人的心全都急得猛跳。船平均每小时前进九英里才有希望，偏偏风在一刻比一刻小！岸上吹来的风反复无常，风过处海面就全平了。可是“坦卡代尔号”船体如此轻盈，船帆对一缕缕来去不定的微风又把握得如此精妙，再添海流相助，六点时，约翰·邦斯比发现他们距上海的入海河口已不超过十英里。上海城本身还得从河口上行至少十二英里。七点钟，他们离上海仍有三英里。引水员愤怒地骂了一声，两百英镑的酬金眼看要飞走了。他望向福克。福克先生一如既往，心平气静；可就在这一刻，押在上头的是他的全副家当。
也就在这一刻，水天相接的地方现出一根黑色的长烟囱，顶上缠着一圈圈煤烟。那便是美国轮船，正按规定时刻动身去横滨。
“见鬼！”约翰·邦斯比绝望地把舵猛推了回去。
“向它发信号。”菲利亚斯·福克平静地说。
“坦卡代尔号”首甲板上立着一门小铜炮，本来为雾中发出信号之用。炮药已装到炮口。就在引水员要把一块红炭凑近火门时，福克先生说：“升旗！”
旗号升到半桅。既然这表示遇险，人们便希望美国轮船看见后肯略偏一点航向，前来救助引水船。
“开火！”福克先生说。小铜炮轰然一响，震动了空气。

sections.title_zh: 第22章　万事通发觉，即使到了地球另一端，口袋里有钱依然方便
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XXII. — IN WHICH PASSEPARTOUT FINDS OUT THAT, EVEN AT THE ANTIPODES, IT IS CONVENIENT TO HAVE SOME MONEY IN ONE’S POCKET
source_paragraphs: The “Carnatic,” setting sail from Hong Kong at half-past six on the 7th of November, directed her course at full steam towards Japan. She carried a large cargo and a well-filled cabin of passengers. Two state-rooms in the rear were, however, unoccupied—those which had been engaged by Phileas Fogg.
The next day a passenger with a half-stupefied eye, staggering gait, and disordered hair, was seen to emerge from the second cabin, and to totter to a seat on deck.

It was Passepartout; and what had happened to him was as follows: Shortly after Fix left the opium den, two waiters had lifted the unconscious Passepartout, and had carried him to the bed reserved for the smokers. Three hours later, pursued even in his dreams by a fixed idea, the poor fellow awoke, and struggled against the stupefying influence of the narcotic. The thought of a duty unfulfilled shook off his torpor, and he hurried from the abode of drunkenness. Staggering and holding himself up by keeping against the walls, falling down and creeping up again, and irresistibly impelled by a kind of instinct, he kept crying out, “The ‘Carnatic!’ the ‘Carnatic!’”

The steamer lay puffing alongside the quay, on the point of starting. Passepartout had but few steps to go; and, rushing upon the plank, he crossed it, and fell unconscious on the deck, just as the “Carnatic” was moving off. Several sailors, who were evidently accustomed to this sort of scene, carried the poor Frenchman down into the second cabin, and Passepartout did not wake until they were one hundred and fifty miles away from China. Thus he found himself the next morning on the deck of the “Carnatic,” and eagerly inhaling the exhilarating sea-breeze. The pure air sobered him. He began to collect his sense, which he found a difficult task; but at last he recalled the events of the evening before, Fix’s revelation, and the opium-house.
“It is evident,” said he to himself, “that I have been abominably drunk! What will Mr. Fogg say? At least I have not missed the steamer, which is the most important thing.”

Then, as Fix occurred to him: “As for that rascal, I hope we are well rid of him, and that he has not dared, as he proposed, to follow us on board the “Carnatic.” A detective on the track of Mr. Fogg, accused of robbing the Bank of England! Pshaw! Mr. Fogg is no more a robber than I am a murderer.”

Should he divulge Fix’s real errand to his master? Would it do to tell the part the detective was playing? Would it not be better to wait until Mr. Fogg reached London again, and then impart to him that an agent of the metropolitan police had been following him round the world, and have a good laugh over it? No doubt; at least, it was worth considering. The first thing to do was to find Mr. Fogg, and apologise for his singular behaviour.

Passepartout got up and proceeded, as well as he could with the rolling of the steamer, to the after-deck. He saw no one who resembled either his master or Aouda. “Good!” muttered he; “Aouda has not got up yet, and Mr. Fogg has probably found some partners at whist.”

He descended to the saloon. Mr. Fogg was not there. Passepartout had only, however, to ask the purser the number of his master’s state-room. The purser replied that he did not know any passenger by the name of Fogg.
“I beg your pardon,” said Passepartout persistently. “He is a tall gentleman, quiet, and not very talkative, and has with him a young lady—”
“There is no young lady on board,” interrupted the purser. “Here is a list of the passengers; you may see for yourself.”
Passepartout scanned the list, but his master’s name was not upon it. All at once an idea struck him.
“Ah! am I on the ‘Carnatic?’”
“Yes.”
“On the way to Yokohama?”
“Certainly.”
Passepartout had for an instant feared that he was on the wrong boat; but, though he was really on the “Carnatic,” his master was not there.

He fell thunderstruck on a seat. He saw it all now. He remembered that the time of sailing had been changed, that he should have informed his master of that fact, and that he had not done so. It was his fault, then, that Mr. Fogg and Aouda had missed the steamer. Yes, but it was still more the fault of the traitor who, in order to separate him from his master, and detain the latter at Hong Kong, had inveigled him into getting drunk! He now saw the detective’s trick; and at this moment Mr. Fogg was certainly ruined, his bet was lost, and he himself perhaps arrested and imprisoned! At this thought Passepartout tore his hair. Ah, if Fix ever came within his reach, what a settling of accounts there would be!

After his first depression, Passepartout became calmer, and began to study his situation. It was certainly not an enviable one. He found himself on the way to Japan, and what should he do when he got there? His pocket was empty; he had not a solitary shilling, not so much as a penny. His passage had fortunately been paid for in advance; and he had five or six days in which to decide upon his future course. He fell to at meals with an appetite, and ate for Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and himself. He helped himself as generously as if Japan were a desert, where nothing to eat was to be looked for.

At dawn on the 13th the “Carnatic” entered the port of Yokohama. This is an important port of call in the Pacific, where all the mail-steamers, and those carrying travellers between North America, China, Japan, and the Oriental islands put in. It is situated in the bay of Yeddo, and at but a short distance from that second capital of the Japanese Empire, and the residence of the Tycoon, the civil Emperor, before the Mikado, the spiritual Emperor, absorbed his office in his own. The “Carnatic” anchored at the quay near the custom-house, in the midst of a crowd of ships bearing the flags of all nations.

Passepartout went timidly ashore on this so curious territory of the Sons of the Sun. He had nothing better to do than, taking chance for his guide, to wander aimlessly through the streets of Yokohama. He found himself at first in a thoroughly European quarter, the houses having low fronts, and being adorned with verandas, beneath which he caught glimpses of neat peristyles. This quarter occupied, with its streets, squares, docks, and warehouses, all the space between the “promontory of the Treaty” and the river. Here, as at Hong Kong and Calcutta, were mixed crowds of all races, Americans and English, Chinamen and Dutchmen, mostly merchants ready to buy or sell anything. The Frenchman felt himself as much alone among them as if he had dropped down in the midst of Hottentots.

He had, at least, one resource,—to call on the French and English consuls at Yokohama for assistance. But he shrank from telling the story of his adventures, intimately connected as it was with that of his master; and, before doing so, he determined to exhaust all other means of aid. As chance did not favour him in the European quarter, he penetrated that inhabited by the native Japanese, determined, if necessary, to push on to Yeddo.

The Japanese quarter of Yokohama is called Benten, after the goddess of the sea, who is worshipped on the islands round about. There Passepartout beheld beautiful fir and cedar groves, sacred gates of a singular architecture, bridges half hid in the midst of bamboos and reeds, temples shaded by immense cedar-trees, holy retreats where were sheltered Buddhist priests and sectaries of Confucius, and interminable streets, where a perfect harvest of rose-tinted and red-cheeked children, who looked as if they had been cut out of Japanese screens, and who were playing in the midst of short-legged poodles and yellowish cats, might have been gathered.

The streets were crowded with people. Priests were passing in processions, beating their dreary tambourines; police and custom-house officers with pointed hats encrusted with lac and carrying two sabres hung to their waists; soldiers, clad in blue cotton with white stripes, and bearing guns; the Mikado’s guards, enveloped in silken doubles, hauberks and coats of mail; and numbers of military folk of all ranks—for the military profession is as much respected in Japan as it is despised in China—went hither and thither in groups and pairs. Passepartout saw, too, begging friars, long-robed pilgrims, and simple civilians, with their warped and jet-black hair, big heads, long busts, slender legs, short stature, and complexions varying from copper-colour to a dead white, but never yellow, like the Chinese, from whom the Japanese widely differ. He did not fail to observe the curious equipages—carriages and palanquins, barrows supplied with sails, and litters made of bamboo; nor the women—whom he thought not especially handsome—who took little steps with their little feet, whereon they wore canvas shoes, straw sandals, and clogs of worked wood, and who displayed tight-looking eyes, flat chests, teeth fashionably blackened, and gowns crossed with silken scarfs, tied in an enormous knot behind an ornament which the modern Parisian ladies seem to have borrowed from the dames of Japan.

Passepartout wandered for several hours in the midst of this motley crowd, looking in at the windows of the rich and curious shops, the jewellery establishments glittering with quaint Japanese ornaments, the restaurants decked with streamers and banners, the tea-houses, where the odorous beverage was being drunk with “saki,” a liquor concocted from the fermentation of rice, and the comfortable smoking-houses, where they were puffing, not opium, which is almost unknown in Japan, but a very fine, stringy tobacco. He went on till he found himself in the fields, in the midst of vast rice plantations. There he saw dazzling camellias expanding themselves, with flowers which were giving forth their last colours and perfumes, not on bushes, but on trees, and within bamboo enclosures, cherry, plum, and apple trees, which the Japanese cultivate rather for their blossoms than their fruit, and which queerly-fashioned, grinning scarecrows protected from the sparrows, pigeons, ravens, and other voracious birds. On the branches of the cedars were perched large eagles; amid the foliage of the weeping willows were herons, solemnly standing on one leg; and on every hand were crows, ducks, hawks, wild birds, and a multitude of cranes, which the Japanese consider sacred, and which to their minds symbolise long life and prosperity.
As he was strolling along, Passepartout espied some violets among the shrubs.
“Good!” said he; “I’ll have some supper.”
But, on smelling them, he found that they were odourless.
“No chance there,” thought he.

The worthy fellow had certainly taken good care to eat as hearty a breakfast as possible before leaving the “Carnatic;” but, as he had been walking about all day, the demands of hunger were becoming importunate. He observed that the butchers stalls contained neither mutton, goat, nor pork; and, knowing also that it is a sacrilege to kill cattle, which are preserved solely for farming, he made up his mind that meat was far from plentiful in Yokohama—nor was he mistaken; and, in default of butcher’s meat, he could have wished for a quarter of wild boar or deer, a partridge, or some quails, some game or fish, which, with rice, the Japanese eat almost exclusively. But he found it necessary to keep up a stout heart, and to postpone the meal he craved till the following morning. Night came, and Passepartout re-entered the native quarter, where he wandered through the streets, lit by vari-coloured lanterns, looking on at the dancers, who were executing skilful steps and boundings, and the astrologers who stood in the open air with their telescopes. Then he came to the harbour, which was lit up by the resin torches of the fishermen, who were fishing from their boats.

The streets at last became quiet, and the patrol, the officers of which, in their splendid costumes, and surrounded by their suites, Passepartout thought seemed like ambassadors, succeeded the bustling crowd. Each time a company passed, Passepartout chuckled, and said to himself: “Good! another Japanese embassy departing for Europe!”
translated_paragraphs: 十一月七日六点半，“卡尔纳蒂克号”离开香港，开足马力，取道日本。船上载有大宗货物，客舱也几乎坐满。只有船尾两间客房空着，那是菲利亚斯·福克订的房间。
第二天，有人看见一个旅客从二等舱里钻出来，目光半痴半醒，头发蓬乱，走路东倒西歪，好不容易才摸到甲板上一张椅子坐下。

正是万事通。事情的来龙去脉如下：菲克斯离开鸦片馆不久，两名伙计把人事不知的万事通抬起来，送上专供烟客躺卧的通铺。过了三个钟头，可怜的家伙醒了。一个念头连在梦里还紧追着他，他醒过来，竭力跟麻醉的药力抗争。那件尚未履行的差事终于把他从昏沉中摇醒。他匆匆逃出这醉生梦死的地方，摇摇晃晃，靠墙支撑着自己。跌倒了，便再爬起来。一种几乎称得上本能的力量，一路不容抗拒地催着他，他不停叫道：“卡尔纳蒂克号！卡尔纳蒂克号！”

轮船在码头边喷着汽，眼看就要启程。万事通只剩几步路。他冲上跳板，刚越过去，就一头栽倒在甲板上，再度失去知觉。就在这一刻，“卡尔纳蒂克号”驶离岸边。好几个水手对这类场面显然已见惯不怪，便把这个可怜的法国人抬下去，送进二等舱。直到船离开中国海岸一百五十英里，万事通才醒来。于是第二天早上，他就在“卡尔纳蒂克号”的甲板上，大口吸着提神的海风。清新的空气使他清醒过来。他开始整理乱成一团的思绪，这事干起来颇为费力；总算，他终于想起头天晚上的经过，想起菲克斯向他透露的身份，也想起了鸦片馆。
“明摆着的，”他对自己说，“我醉得简直不像样了！福克先生会怎么说？至少轮船我没有错过，这可是头等大事。”
接着想到菲克斯，他又说：“至于那坏蛋，但愿我们已把他甩得远远的，但愿他没胆量照他自己原先提的那样，追着我们登上‘卡尔纳蒂克号’。竟有个警探跟踪福克先生，说他偷了英格兰银行！呸！说福克先生是贼，跟说我是个杀人犯一样荒唐。”
要不要把菲克斯真正执行什么差事，告诉主人？要不要告知那个警探在扮演什么角色？还是等福克回到伦敦再讲，说伦敦警察厅派出一人，足足跟着他绕了地球一周，大家到时候放声笑上一回，岂不更好？的确如此，至少值得考虑。不过眼下的第一桩事，是赶快找着福克先生，为自己那番古怪行径道歉。
万事通站起来，尽力在颠簸中站稳，朝后甲板走去。他没看见一个像主人的人，也没看见艾娥达。“好吧，”他喃喃道，“艾娥达一定还没起床。至于福克先生，多半已找到几位惠斯特牌搭子了。”
他下到客厅舱。福克先生不在那里。不过他只需要向事务长打听一下主人的舱号就行了。事务长却答道，他可不认识哪位姓福克的乘客。
“请原谅，”万事通坚持道，“他是位高个子绅士，安安静静，不太说话。跟他在一起的还有一位年轻女士——”
“船上没有年轻女士，”事务长打断了他，“旅客名册在这里，你可以自己看。”
万事通细查名册，可没有主人的名字。猛然间，他生出一个念头。
“啊！我搭的，是‘卡尔纳蒂克号’吗？”
“是的。”
“开往横滨？”
“当然。”
刚才有那么一瞬，万事通还怕自己上错了船。可他上的当真是“卡尔纳蒂克号”，主人却不在船上。

他像遭了雷击，瘫坐在一张椅子上。这下什么都明白了。他记起轮船的开航时间提前了，自己本该向主人报告，却没有去。如此说来，福克先生和艾娥达错过轮船，责任在他。是呀，不过那个叛徒的罪过更大。为了把他跟主人拆开，把主人拖在香港，那人竟蓄意哄他喝醉！警探使的什么诡计，他现在总算看清了。可眼下福克先生必已彻底破产，赌约必已输了，没准连人也已被捕入狱！想到这儿，万事通双手揪着自己的头发。啊，菲克斯只要有朝一日再落到他手里，看他会怎样跟这家伙算总账！
最初那阵消沉过去，万事通稍稍冷静，开始审视自己的处境。实在不是个值得羡慕的处境。他正在去日本的路上，可到了那里该怎么办？口袋已空，没有一个先令，甚至没有一便士。还好船费已预先付过，他还有五六天工夫来决定今后的打算。到了吃饭时，他很有胃口，简直把福克先生、艾娥达和自己三个人的份都吃了。那副毫不亏待自己的架势，活像日本是一片找不到半点吃食的荒漠。
十三日清晨，“卡尔纳蒂克号”进入横滨港。这是太平洋上的一个重要停靠港，各路邮轮以及在北美、中国、日本和东方诸岛之间运送旅客的轮船，都在此停泊。它坐落于江户湾，离日本帝国的那座第二都城不远。过去，掌管世俗政务的大君，也就是幕府将军，驻在江户；后来，作为精神领袖的天皇将他的职权也收归自己手下。“卡尔纳蒂克号”停靠在海关附近的码头，周围船只密集，飘着各国旗帜。

万事通怯生生地踏上了太阳子民这片如此新奇的土地。别无更好的事可做，他便把偶然当作向导，无目的地漫步在横滨街头。最初，他置身于一个彻底欧化的城区。房子临街的一面较低，带着游廊，廊下可以望见整齐的柱廊。街道、广场、船坞和仓库占满了所谓“条约岬”与河流之间的整个地带。跟香港、加尔各答一样，各种族群都混在这里，有美国人、英国人、中国人、荷兰人，大多是商人，什么都愿意买卖。可是法国人夹在他们中间，只觉得自己孤零零的，仿佛一下子掉进了非洲南部的科伊科伊人中间。
至少他还有一条路：向法国或英国驻横滨领事求助。可他的历险同主人的事纠缠得太紧，他不愿把它们讲出来。除非别的求助办法全都用尽，他不会这样做。欧洲人居住的区域没带给他什么好运，他便钻进日本人居住的城区，打定主意，有必要时就一路走到江户。
横滨的日本城区叫弁天，取的是周围岛屿所奉海神的名字。在那儿，万事通瞧见了秀美的杉林和雪松林，形制奇特的神门，半掩在竹丛和芦苇里的桥，巨杉浓荫下的寺院，供佛教僧侣和孔门弟子安居的清修之处，还有一条条望不到尽头的街。街上随处都可收获一大群面色粉红、双颊红扑扑的孩子，活像是从日本屏风上剪下来的，正跟短腿的小卷毛狗和发黄的小猫玩成一团。

街上人流熙攘。僧人结队走过，敲着单调的手鼓。戴尖顶漆帽的警员和海关人员，腰间各悬两把刀。士兵穿蓝地白条的棉布衣，背着枪。天皇的卫士身着丝绸短褂、护身锁甲和甲胄。各个等级的武人，或三五成群，或两两作伴，四下穿行；在这里，军人的职业受到尊重，而在中国却受轻视，这正是两国的不同。万事通还看见托钵的僧人、长袍的朝圣者和普通市民。他们束着乌黑的发髻，脑袋大，身躯长，腿细，个头不高，肤色从古铜色到苍白色都有。他眼中的日本人同中国人很不相同，肤色中没有他所谓中国人的黄色。他没漏看那些新奇的交通工具：马车、轿子、张着风帆的独轮车，以及用竹子做的抬轿。妇女们他也看了。他觉得她们算不得格外美貌，纤足迈着细碎小步，脚上穿帆布鞋、草鞋或雕制的木屐。她们眼形狭长，胸脯平坦，依时尚把牙齿染黑，袍服在胸前相掩，丝绸腰带在背后结成一个大结。如今巴黎太太们的装饰，仿佛正是向日本妇人借来的。

万事通在这形形色色的人群中兜了几个钟头，隔着橱窗往里望。店铺富丽而新奇；珠宝店里，日本样式别致的首饰熠熠生辉；饭馆挂着彩带旗幡；茶馆里，人们品着散发清香的茶，也喝着米酿发酵的清酒。舒适的烟馆里，人们喷云吐雾，抽的却不是在日本几乎见不到的鸦片，而是极细的丝状烟草。他不停往前走，一直来到乡野，身边已是大片稻田。他望见色彩灿烂的山茶树正在开花。花不长在小灌木上，而在大树上绽放出这一季最后的色泽和香气。竹篱里种着樱树、梅树和苹果树。日本人栽它们，重赏花胜过收果。形状奇怪、龇牙咧嘴的稻草人守着树木，以防麻雀、鸽子、渡鸦和其余贪吃的鸟。大鹰栖在雪松枝上，垂柳间，苍鹭庄重地单腿独立。四面还有乌鸦、野鸭、鹰隼、各种野鸟，和大量的鹤。日本人视鹤为神圣的生灵，把它看作长寿和兴旺的象征。
漫步之中，万事通瞥见灌木丛里有些紫罗兰。
“好极啦！”他说，“晚饭有着落了。”
可他凑近闻了闻，发现这些花没有香气。
“那就没指望了。”他暗想。

离开“卡尔纳蒂克号”以前，这个好心人确实十分有远见，尽可能吃了顿饱饱的早饭。可他毕竟已走了整天，肚子的催讨现在变得很不客气。他发现肉铺摊上不见绵羊、山羊或猪肉，又听说在这里牛只养来耕田，宰牛是亵渎之举，便断定横滨的肉食远非充裕；这倒没有猜错。没有普通肉铺卖的肉，他也巴不得来四分之一扇野猪或鹿肉，一只山鹑，或几只鹌鹑。来点野味或鱼都好；这些配着米饭，几乎就是日本人全部的饮食。不过他发现，眼下还是非得打起精神，等明早再来张罗这顿心心念念的饭。夜色降临，他走回日本城区，漫步在用各色灯笼照亮的街上。他看舞者施展灵巧的舞步，一跃而起，又看占星人在露天架起望远镜。再走到港口，只见渔夫坐在小船上垂钓，松脂火把照亮了港湾。
到了最后，街上终于安静下来。原来熙熙攘攘的人群退去，巡逻队接班。那些带队的军官装束华丽，周围前呼后拥，万事通觉得他们俨然是出使的大使。每有一队经过，他就独自窃笑，心里说：“好！又是一支日本使团出发上欧洲去啦！”

sections.title_zh: 第23章　万事通的鼻子长到荒唐的地步
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XXIII. — IN WHICH PASSEPARTOUT’S NOSE BECOMES OUTRAGEOUSLY LONG
source_paragraphs: The next morning poor, jaded, famished Passepartout said to himself that he must get something to eat at all hazards, and the sooner he did so the better. He might, indeed, sell his watch; but he would have starved first. Now or never he must use the strong, if not melodious voice which nature had bestowed upon him. He knew several French and English songs, and resolved to try them upon the Japanese, who must be lovers of music, since they were for ever pounding on their cymbals, tam-tams, and tambourines, and could not but appreciate European talent.

It was, perhaps, rather early in the morning to get up a concert, and the audience prematurely aroused from their slumbers, might not possibly pay their entertainer with coin bearing the Mikado’s features. Passepartout therefore decided to wait several hours; and, as he was sauntering along, it occurred to him that he would seem rather too well dressed for a wandering artist. The idea struck him to change his garments for clothes more in harmony with his project; by which he might also get a little money to satisfy the immediate cravings of hunger. The resolution taken, it remained to carry it out.

It was only after a long search that Passepartout discovered a native dealer in old clothes, to whom he applied for an exchange. The man liked the European costume, and ere long Passepartout issued from his shop accoutred in an old Japanese coat, and a sort of one-sided turban, faded with long use. A few small pieces of silver, moreover, jingled in his pocket.
“Good!” thought he. “I will imagine I am at the Carnival!”

His first care, after being thus “Japanesed,” was to enter a tea-house of modest appearance, and, upon half a bird and a little rice, to breakfast like a man for whom dinner was as yet a problem to be solved.

“Now,” thought he, when he had eaten heartily, “I mustn’t lose my head. I can’t sell this costume again for one still more Japanese. I must consider how to leave this country of the Sun, of which I shall not retain the most delightful of memories, as quickly as possible.”

It occurred to him to visit the steamers which were about to leave for America. He would offer himself as a cook or servant, in payment of his passage and meals. Once at San Francisco, he would find some means of going on. The difficulty was, how to traverse the four thousand seven hundred miles of the Pacific which lay between Japan and the New World.

Passepartout was not the man to let an idea go begging, and directed his steps towards the docks. But, as he approached them, his project, which at first had seemed so simple, began to grow more and more formidable to his mind. What need would they have of a cook or servant on an American steamer, and what confidence would they put in him, dressed as he was? What references could he give?
As he was reflecting in this wise, his eyes fell upon an immense placard which a sort of clown was carrying through the streets. This placard, which was in English, read as follows:

ACROBATIC JAPANESE TROUPE,
HONOURABLE WILLIAM BATULCAR, PROPRIETOR,
LAST REPRESENTATIONS,
PRIOR TO THEIR DEPARTURE TO THE UNITED STATES,
OF THE
LONG NOSES! LONG NOSES!
UNDER THE DIRECT PATRONAGE OF THE GOD TINGOU!
GREAT ATTRACTION!
“The United States!” said Passepartout; “that’s just what I want!”

He followed the clown, and soon found himself once more in the Japanese quarter. A quarter of an hour later he stopped before a large cabin, adorned with several clusters of streamers, the exterior walls of which were designed to represent, in violent colours and without perspective, a company of jugglers.

This was the Honourable William Batulcar’s establishment. That gentleman was a sort of Barnum, the director of a troupe of mountebanks, jugglers, clowns, acrobats, equilibrists, and gymnasts, who, according to the placard, was giving his last performances before leaving the Empire of the Sun for the States of the Union.
Passepartout entered and asked for Mr. Batulcar, who straightway appeared in person.
“What do you want?” said he to Passepartout, whom he at first took for a native.
“Would you like a servant, sir?” asked Passepartout.

“A servant!” cried Mr. Batulcar, caressing the thick grey beard which hung from his chin. “I already have two who are obedient and faithful, have never left me, and serve me for their nourishment and here they are,” added he, holding out his two robust arms, furrowed with veins as large as the strings of a bass-viol.
“So I can be of no use to you?”
“None.”
“The devil! I should so like to cross the Pacific with you!”
“Ah!” said the Honourable Mr. Batulcar. “You are no more a Japanese than I am a monkey! Who are you dressed up in that way?”
“A man dresses as he can.”
“That’s true. You are a Frenchman, aren’t you?”
“Yes; a Parisian of Paris.”
“Then you ought to know how to make grimaces?”
“Why,” replied Passepartout, a little vexed that his nationality should cause this question, “we Frenchmen know how to make grimaces, it is true but not any better than the Americans do.”
“True. Well, if I can’t take you as a servant, I can as a clown. You see, my friend, in France they exhibit foreign clowns, and in foreign parts French clowns.”
“Ah!”
“You are pretty strong, eh?”
“Especially after a good meal.”
“And you can sing?”
“Yes,” returned Passepartout, who had formerly been wont to sing in the streets.
“But can you sing standing on your head, with a top spinning on your left foot, and a sabre balanced on your right?”
“Humph! I think so,” replied Passepartout, recalling the exercises of his younger days.
“Well, that’s enough,” said the Honourable William Batulcar.
The engagement was concluded there and then.

Passepartout had at last found something to do. He was engaged to act in the celebrated Japanese troupe. It was not a very dignified position, but within a week he would be on his way to San Francisco.

The performance, so noisily announced by the Honourable Mr. Batulcar, was to commence at three o’clock, and soon the deafening instruments of a Japanese orchestra resounded at the door. Passepartout, though he had not been able to study or rehearse a part, was designated to lend the aid of his sturdy shoulders in the great exhibition of the “human pyramid,” executed by the Long Noses of the god Tingou. This “great attraction” was to close the performance.

Before three o’clock the large shed was invaded by the spectators, comprising Europeans and natives, Chinese and Japanese, men, women and children, who precipitated themselves upon the narrow benches and into the boxes opposite the stage. The musicians took up a position inside, and were vigorously performing on their gongs, tam-tams, flutes, bones, tambourines, and immense drums.
The performance was much like all acrobatic displays; but it must be confessed that the Japanese are the first equilibrists in the world.

One, with a fan and some bits of paper, performed the graceful trick of the butterflies and the flowers; another traced in the air, with the odorous smoke of his pipe, a series of blue words, which composed a compliment to the audience; while a third juggled with some lighted candles, which he extinguished successively as they passed his lips, and relit again without interrupting for an instant his juggling. Another reproduced the most singular combinations with a spinning-top; in his hands the revolving tops seemed to be animated with a life of their own in their interminable whirling; they ran over pipe-stems, the edges of sabres, wires and even hairs stretched across the stage; they turned around on the edges of large glasses, crossed bamboo ladders, dispersed into all the corners, and produced strange musical effects by the combination of their various pitches of tone. The jugglers tossed them in the air, threw them like shuttlecocks with wooden battledores, and yet they kept on spinning; they put them into their pockets, and took them out still whirling as before.
It is useless to describe the astonishing performances of the acrobats and gymnasts. The turning on ladders, poles, balls, barrels, &c., was executed with wonderful precision.
But the principal attraction was the exhibition of the Long Noses, a show to which Europe is as yet a stranger.

The Long Noses form a peculiar company, under the direct patronage of the god Tingou. Attired after the fashion of the Middle Ages, they bore upon their shoulders a splendid pair of wings; but what especially distinguished them was the long noses which were fastened to their faces, and the uses which they made of them. These noses were made of bamboo, and were five, six, and even ten feet long, some straight, others curved, some ribboned, and some having imitation warts upon them. It was upon these appendages, fixed tightly on their real noses, that they performed their gymnastic exercises. A dozen of these sectaries of Tingou lay flat upon their backs, while others, dressed to represent lightning-rods, came and frolicked on their noses, jumping from one to another, and performing the most skilful leapings and somersaults.

As a last scene, a “human pyramid” had been announced, in which fifty Long Noses were to represent the Car of Juggernaut. But, instead of forming a pyramid by mounting each other’s shoulders, the artists were to group themselves on top of the noses. It happened that the performer who had hitherto formed the base of the Car had quitted the troupe, and as, to fill this part, only strength and adroitness were necessary, Passepartout had been chosen to take his place.

The poor fellow really felt sad when—melancholy reminiscence of his youth!—he donned his costume, adorned with vari-coloured wings, and fastened to his natural feature a false nose six feet long. But he cheered up when he thought that this nose was winning him something to eat.

He went upon the stage, and took his place beside the rest who were to compose the base of the Car of Juggernaut. They all stretched themselves on the floor, their noses pointing to the ceiling. A second group of artists disposed themselves on these long appendages, then a third above these, then a fourth, until a human monument reaching to the very cornices of the theatre soon arose on top of the noses. This elicited loud applause, in the midst of which the orchestra was just striking up a deafening air, when the pyramid tottered, the balance was lost, one of the lower noses vanished from the pyramid, and the human monument was shattered like a castle built of cards!

It was Passepartout’s fault. Abandoning his position, clearing the footlights without the aid of his wings, and, clambering up to the right-hand gallery, he fell at the feet of one of the spectators, crying, “Ah, my master! my master!”
“You here?”
“Myself.”
“Very well; then let us go to the steamer, young man!”

Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout passed through the lobby of the theatre to the outside, where they encountered the Honourable Mr. Batulcar, furious with rage. He demanded damages for the “breakage” of the pyramid; and Phileas Fogg appeased him by giving him a handful of banknotes.
At half-past six, the very hour of departure, Mr. Fogg and Aouda, followed by Passepartout, who in his hurry had retained his wings, and nose six feet long, stepped upon the American steamer.
translated_paragraphs: 次日清早，万事通又累又饿，十分可怜。他告诉自己，不管冒什么险，先得弄点吃的，越快越好。他本来也可以卖了表。可他宁愿先饿死。这下，天生给他的那副嗓子非派上用场不可了：音色未必悦耳，声音可够洪亮。他会唱几首法国歌和英国歌，决定唱给日本人试试。日本人成天地敲钹、打锣、摇铃鼓，一定爱好音乐，也一定懂得欣赏欧洲人的才艺。
不过一大早开音乐会，兴许为时过早。听众们过早地被从睡梦里吵醒，只怕未必愿意掏出铸着天皇像的硬币答谢艺人。万事通决定再等几小时。他一面踱着步子，一面忽然想到：作一个流浪卖艺者，自己穿得似乎太讲究了些。何不把身上的衣服换一套更合这个行当的？兴许还能得一点钱，先满足肚子眼下的急需。主意打定，只剩动手实行。
找了好半天，万事通才发现一个本地旧衣商，向他开口说想换身衣裳。商人很喜欢他的欧式服装。没一会儿，万事通再出店门，已经穿上一件旧日本外褂，头上歪戴着一种用旧了、褪了色的包头巾。此外，口袋里还叮当响着几枚小银币。
“好极了！”他想，“我只当自己是来过狂欢节的！”
这一番“日本化”以后，他的第一件事便是钻进一间模样朴实的茶馆，用半只禽鸟和一点米饭吃顿早饭。看他的吃法，就知道这人下一顿饭从哪儿来，还是个有待解决的问题。
肚子吃得踏实了，他想：“现在我可不能昏了头。这身行头总不能再卖一回，换套更日本的吧。得想想怎么快快离开这个太阳之国，它给我留下的回忆，可称不上特别甜美。”
他想到，可以去打听有哪些轮船就要开往美洲，自己拿当厨子或当仆人的工钱抵船票和饭钱。一旦到了旧金山，总会想到再走下去的办法。难就难在日本与新大陆之间，横着太平洋四千七百英里的水路，怎样才能过去？
万事通从不让想出的主意白白搁着，举步便向码头走去。可是离码头越近，起初看起来极容易的计划，便在心里越发显得困难重重。美国轮船哪里就缺个厨子或仆人？再看自己打扮成这副模样，谁肯信他？他又拿得出什么可靠的推荐？
正这么琢磨着，他的目光落在一张硕大的招贴上。一个打扮近似小丑的人，正扛着它沿街走过。招贴用英文写道：

日本杂技团
尊敬的威廉·巴图尔卡先生主办
启程前往美利坚合众国之前
最后几场隆重献演
长鼻子！长鼻子！
天狗神亲自庇护！
不可错过的精彩奇观！
“美利坚合众国！”万事通说，“这正合我意！”
他尾随小丑，不久已再次来到日本城区。一刻钟后，他在一座大棚前停下。棚上装饰着几大簇彩带，外墙上用极鲜艳的色彩画出一群杂耍艺人，至于远近透视，那是半点也不讲究。
这是尊敬的威廉·巴图尔卡先生的产业。这位先生是个巴纳姆式的人物，手下有一班卖艺人、魔术师、小丑、杂技演员、平衡艺人和体操能手。据招贴所说，在离开太阳帝国前往美利坚联邦各州之前，他们正在做最后几场演出。
万事通进门要求面见巴图尔卡先生。那位先生随即亲自出现。
“你想干什么？”他问万事通，开头把万事通当成了本地人。
“先生，您缺个仆人吗？”万事通问。
“仆人！”巴图尔卡先生摸摸颏下浓密的灰胡子，叫了起来，“我已经有两个了，听话、忠心，一直没离开过我，只要赏它们一口饭就肯服侍。你瞧，都在这里呢。”说着，他伸出两条粗壮的胳膊，上面青筋隆起，粗得像低音维奥尔琴上的弦。
“这么说，我帮不上您什么忙？”
“帮不上。”
“见鬼！我真想跟着您一道横渡太平洋！”
“啊！”尊敬的巴图尔卡先生说，“要说你是日本人，那我就是只猴子了！你这身打扮底下，到底是什么人？”
“人有怎样的衣裳，就只能穿怎样的衣裳。”
“这倒是实话。你是法国人吧？”
“是呀，地地道道的巴黎人。”
“那你一定很会扮鬼脸喽？”
“唔，”只因为他是法国人便这么问，万事通略有些恼火，“我们法国人确实会扮鬼脸，可也不比美国人高明。”
“说得是。我不能雇你来作仆人，却可以雇你来当小丑。朋友，你知道，在法国上台的是外国小丑，到了外国，又该轮到法国小丑上台。”
“你身上颇有把子力气，是不是？”
“尤其是在吃过一顿饱饭以后。”
“会唱歌吗？”
“会。”万事通答道。从前他在街上卖唱，本来就是常事。
“那你能不能头朝下倒立着唱，左脚顶个旋转的陀螺，右脚再平衡一把军刀？”
“嗯！我想可以。”万事通答道，想起自己年轻时练过的本领。
“很好，那就够了。”尊敬的威廉·巴图尔卡说。
这笔聘用交易当场谈妥。
万事通终于有事可做了。他受雇在这个著名的日本杂技团中演出。这个职位谈不上多么体面，可用不了一星期，他就可以踏上去旧金山的路。
巴图尔卡先生如此大张旗鼓宣传的演出，定在三点钟开场。不久，日本乐队震耳欲聋的乐声已在门口响起。万事通来不及学角色，也没法排练；不过他的双肩强壮，已被指定去给一项大型表演出力。天狗神的长鼻子们要叠一座“人塔”，整场演出将以这项“精彩奇观”压轴。
还不到三点，大棚里已经涌满观众。欧洲人和当地人混在一处，中国人、日本人，男人、女人、孩子，纷纷扑向狭窄的长凳，或挤进舞台对面的包厢。乐师们移到棚里，卖力地敲起大锣、小锣、骨响板、铃鼓和大得惊人的鼓，间有笛声掺在其中。
开场的节目跟寻常杂技演出大体相仿。可是讲到平衡术，可得承认，日本艺人真称得上世界第一。

有一个人用一把扇子和几小片纸，变出优美的花蝶戏；另一个从烟管里喷出带香味的烟，在空中写成一串蓝色的字，是向观众致意的话。第三个抛接着几支燃烧的蜡烛，每支从唇边经过时便吹灭，转眼又把它点燃，一整套抛接动作一刻也不间断。还有一人让陀螺变出最奇特的花样。在他手里，那些陀螺旋转不息，仿佛有自己的性命似的；它们滚过烟管，走上军刀的刃口，沿细铁丝前进，甚至能沿着横跨舞台的一根发丝走过去。它们绕着大杯的杯口打转，越过竹梯，四散飞往各个角落；转起来各有音高，合在一起便能奏出奇妙的乐声。艺人们把它们抛向半空，又用木球拍像拍羽毛球一样将它们拍出去。陀螺照旧打转。他们把它们放进口袋，再取出来，仍转得跟方才一样快。
至于杂技艺人和体操能手那些叫人吃惊的本领，实在不必再一一描写。他们在梯上、杆上、球上、木桶上翻转腾挪，每一手都准确得惊人。
可是最吸引人的，仍数长鼻子们的表演，这种节目欧洲至今还没见识过。

长鼻子们自成一个奇特的团体，受天狗神直接庇护。他们作中古时代的装扮，肩上披一对华美的翅膀。可最使他们与众不同的，还是牢牢绑在脸上的长鼻子，以及他们使用它的种种法子。这些鼻子用竹子做成，长五英尺、六英尺，甚至十英尺。有的是直的，有的是弯的；有的缠着彩带，有的贴着假疣子。他们正是凭这些固定在真鼻子上的附件来表演体操。十二个天狗信徒仰面平躺，另一些人打扮成避雷针的样子，在他们的鼻子上蹦跳嬉戏，从这一根纵身跃往另一根，接连表演最灵巧的跳跃和空翻。
压轴的节目已经预告过了，叫“人塔”。五十个长鼻子要合作摆出贾格纳特神车的模样。艺人们叠塔并不一个个爬上旁人的肩，而要分层立在鼻尖上。碰巧，原来在神车最底下一层打底的演员刚离团。这个角色只需要力气和敏捷，因此万事通给选来顶替他。
穿上缀有五色翅膀的行头，把一根长六英尺的假鼻子安在自己天生的鼻子上时，万事通不由得一阵伤感：这模样，多叫他想起少年时的旧日子！不过一想到正是这根鼻子替他赢来了饭吃，他的精神又振作了起来。
万事通走上舞台，同其余几个负责给贾格纳特神车打底的人并排就位。所有人都躺平，鼻子直指天花板。第二层艺人在那些长家伙上各自就位，再往上是第三层、第四层。不多时，一座直抵剧棚顶檐的人体纪念碑，已从鼻子们的尖端拔地而起。满场响起热烈的掌声。乐队正奏出一支震耳欲聋的曲子，不料人塔一晃，顿失平衡，最底层竟抽走了一根鼻子。整座人体纪念碑就像扑克牌搭的城堡一样，哗啦啦全塌了！
祸是万事通闯的。他擅离岗位，没借翅膀的力就一跃跳过台口脚灯，手脚并用爬上右边楼座，扑倒在一位观众的脚前，大叫道：“啊，主人！我的主人！”
“你在这里？”
“是我本人。”
“很好。那么，年轻人，我们去搭轮船吧！”
福克先生、艾娥达和万事通穿过剧场门厅走到外头，迎面撞上尊敬的威廉·巴图尔卡先生。他已气得七窍生烟，索要“摔碎”了人塔的赔偿。菲利亚斯·福克给了他一把钞票，平息了他的怒气。
六点半，正是开船时刻，福克先生和艾娥达登上了美国轮船。万事通紧跟其后，匆忙间，肩上还留着那对翅膀，脸上还挺着那根足有六英尺长的鼻子。

sections.title_zh: 第24章　福克先生一行横渡太平洋
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XXIV. — DURING WHICH MR. FOGG AND PARTY CROSS THE PACIFIC OCEAN
source_paragraphs: What happened when the pilot-boat came in sight of Shanghai will be easily guessed. The signals made by the “Tankadere” had been seen by the captain of the Yokohama steamer, who, espying the flag at half-mast, had directed his course towards the little craft. Phileas Fogg, after paying the stipulated price of his passage to John Busby, and rewarding that worthy with the additional sum of five hundred and fifty pounds, ascended the steamer with Aouda and Fix; and they started at once for Nagasaki and Yokohama.

They reached their destination on the morning of the 14th of November. Phileas Fogg lost no time in going on board the “Carnatic,” where he learned, to Aouda’s great delight—and perhaps to his own, though he betrayed no emotion—that Passepartout, a Frenchman, had really arrived on her the day before.

The San Francisco steamer was announced to leave that very evening, and it became necessary to find Passepartout, if possible, without delay. Mr. Fogg applied in vain to the French and English consuls, and, after wandering through the streets a long time, began to despair of finding his missing servant. Chance, or perhaps a kind of presentiment, at last led him into the Honourable Mr. Batulcar’s theatre. He certainly would not have recognised Passepartout in the eccentric mountebank’s costume; but the latter, lying on his back, perceived his master in the gallery. He could not help starting, which so changed the position of his nose as to bring the “pyramid” pell-mell upon the stage.
All this Passepartout learned from Aouda, who recounted to him what had taken place on the voyage from Hong Kong to Shanghai on the “Tankadere,” in company with one Mr. Fix.

Passepartout did not change countenance on hearing this name. He thought that the time had not yet arrived to divulge to his master what had taken place between the detective and himself; and, in the account he gave of his absence, he simply excused himself for having been overtaken by drunkenness, in smoking opium at a tavern in Hong Kong.

Mr. Fogg heard this narrative coldly, without a word; and then furnished his man with funds necessary to obtain clothing more in harmony with his position. Within an hour the Frenchman had cut off his nose and parted with his wings, and retained nothing about him which recalled the sectary of the god Tingou.

The steamer which was about to depart from Yokohama to San Francisco belonged to the Pacific Mail Steamship Company, and was named the “General Grant.” She was a large paddle-wheel steamer of two thousand five hundred tons; well equipped and very fast. The massive walking-beam rose and fell above the deck; at one end a piston-rod worked up and down; and at the other was a connecting-rod which, in changing the rectilinear motion to a circular one, was directly connected with the shaft of the paddles. The “General Grant” was rigged with three masts, giving a large capacity for sails, and thus materially aiding the steam power. By making twelve miles an hour, she would cross the ocean in twenty-one days. Phileas Fogg was therefore justified in hoping that he would reach San Francisco by the 2nd of December, New York by the 11th, and London on the 20th—thus gaining several hours on the fatal date of the 21st of December.

There was a full complement of passengers on board, among them English, many Americans, a large number of coolies on their way to California, and several East Indian officers, who were spending their vacation in making the tour of the world. Nothing of moment happened on the voyage; the steamer, sustained on its large paddles, rolled but little, and the “Pacific” almost justified its name. Mr. Fogg was as calm and taciturn as ever. His young companion felt herself more and more attached to him by other ties than gratitude; his silent but generous nature impressed her more than she thought; and it was almost unconsciously that she yielded to emotions which did not seem to have the least effect upon her protector. Aouda took the keenest interest in his plans, and became impatient at any incident which seemed likely to retard his journey.

She often chatted with Passepartout, who did not fail to perceive the state of the lady’s heart; and, being the most faithful of domestics, he never exhausted his eulogies of Phileas Fogg’s honesty, generosity, and devotion. He took pains to calm Aouda’s doubts of a successful termination of the journey, telling her that the most difficult part of it had passed, that now they were beyond the fantastic countries of Japan and China, and were fairly on their way to civilised places again. A railway train from San Francisco to New York, and a transatlantic steamer from New York to Liverpool, would doubtless bring them to the end of this impossible journey round the world within the period agreed upon.

On the ninth day after leaving Yokohama, Phileas Fogg had traversed exactly one half of the terrestrial globe. The “General Grant” passed, on the 23rd of November, the one hundred and eightieth meridian, and was at the very antipodes of London. Mr. Fogg had, it is true, exhausted fifty-two of the eighty days in which he was to complete the tour, and there were only twenty-eight left. But, though he was only half-way by the difference of meridians, he had really gone over two-thirds of the whole journey; for he had been obliged to make long circuits from London to Aden, from Aden to Bombay, from Calcutta to Singapore, and from Singapore to Yokohama. Could he have followed without deviation the fiftieth parallel, which is that of London, the whole distance would only have been about twelve thousand miles; whereas he would be forced, by the irregular methods of locomotion, to traverse twenty-six thousand, of which he had, on the 23rd of November, accomplished seventeen thousand five hundred. And now the course was a straight one, and Fix was no longer there to put obstacles in their way!

It happened also, on the 23rd of November, that Passepartout made a joyful discovery. It will be remembered that the obstinate fellow had insisted on keeping his famous family watch at London time, and on regarding that of the countries he had passed through as quite false and unreliable. Now, on this day, though he had not changed the hands, he found that his watch exactly agreed with the ship’s chronometers. His triumph was hilarious. He would have liked to know what Fix would say if he were aboard!

“The rogue told me a lot of stories,” repeated Passepartout, “about the meridians, the sun, and the moon! Moon, indeed! moonshine more likely! If one listened to that sort of people, a pretty sort of time one would keep! I was sure that the sun would some day regulate itself by my watch!”

Passepartout was ignorant that, if the face of his watch had been divided into twenty-four hours, like the Italian clocks, he would have no reason for exultation; for the hands of his watch would then, instead of as now indicating nine o’clock in the morning, indicate nine o’clock in the evening, that is, the twenty-first hour after midnight precisely the difference between London time and that of the one hundred and eightieth meridian. But if Fix had been able to explain this purely physical effect, Passepartout would not have admitted, even if he had comprehended it. Moreover, if the detective had been on board at that moment, Passepartout would have joined issue with him on a quite different subject, and in an entirely different manner.
Where was Fix at that moment?
He was actually on board the “General Grant.”

On reaching Yokohama, the detective, leaving Mr. Fogg, whom he expected to meet again during the day, had repaired at once to the English consulate, where he at last found the warrant of arrest. It had followed him from Bombay, and had come by the “Carnatic,” on which steamer he himself was supposed to be. Fix’s disappointment may be imagined when he reflected that the warrant was now useless. Mr. Fogg had left English ground, and it was now necessary to procure his extradition!

“Well,” thought Fix, after a moment of anger, “my warrant is not good here, but it will be in England. The rogue evidently intends to return to his own country, thinking he has thrown the police off his track. Good! I will follow him across the Atlantic. As for the money, heaven grant there may be some left! But the fellow has already spent in travelling, rewards, trials, bail, elephants, and all sorts of charges, more than five thousand pounds. Yet, after all, the Bank is rich!”

His course decided on, he went on board the “General Grant,” and was there when Mr. Fogg and Aouda arrived. To his utter amazement, he recognised Passepartout, despite his theatrical disguise. He quickly concealed himself in his cabin, to avoid an awkward explanation, and hoped—thanks to the number of passengers—to remain unperceived by Mr. Fogg’s servant.

On that very day, however, he met Passepartout face to face on the forward deck. The latter, without a word, made a rush for him, grasped him by the throat, and, much to the amusement of a group of Americans, who immediately began to bet on him, administered to the detective a perfect volley of blows, which proved the great superiority of French over English pugilistic skill.
When Passepartout had finished, he found himself relieved and comforted. Fix got up in a somewhat rumpled condition, and, looking at his adversary, coldly said, “Have you done?”
“For this time—yes.”
“Then let me have a word with you.”
“But I—”
“In your master’s interests.”
Passepartout seemed to be vanquished by Fix’s coolness, for he quietly followed him, and they sat down aside from the rest of the passengers.
“You have given me a thrashing,” said Fix. “Good, I expected it. Now, listen to me. Up to this time I have been Mr. Fogg’s adversary. I am now in his game.”
“Aha!” cried Passepartout; “you are convinced he is an honest man?”

“No,” replied Fix coldly, “I think him a rascal. Sh! don’t budge, and let me speak. As long as Mr. Fogg was on English ground, it was for my interest to detain him there until my warrant of arrest arrived. I did everything I could to keep him back. I sent the Bombay priests after him, I got you intoxicated at Hong Kong, I separated you from him, and I made him miss the Yokohama steamer.”
Passepartout listened, with closed fists.

“Now,” resumed Fix, “Mr. Fogg seems to be going back to England. Well, I will follow him there. But hereafter I will do as much to keep obstacles out of his way as I have done up to this time to put them in his path. I’ve changed my game, you see, and simply because it was for my interest to change it. Your interest is the same as mine; for it is only in England that you will ascertain whether you are in the service of a criminal or an honest man.”
Passepartout listened very attentively to Fix, and was convinced that he spoke with entire good faith.
“Are we friends?” asked the detective.
“Friends?—no,” replied Passepartout; “but allies, perhaps. At the least sign of treason, however, I’ll twist your neck for you.”
“Agreed,” said the detective quietly.
Eleven days later, on the 3rd of December, the “General Grant” entered the bay of the Golden Gate, and reached San Francisco.
Mr. Fogg had neither gained nor lost a single day.
translated_paragraphs: 引水船望见上海以后出了什么事，不难猜到。“坦卡代尔号”发出的信号，开往横滨的轮船船长已经看见。一瞧见半桅悬旗，他就调整航向，驶近小帆船。菲利亚斯·福克照约付了约翰·邦斯比船费，又另外给了这好汉五百五十英镑酬金，随即与艾娥达、菲克斯一同登上大船，立刻向长崎和横滨启程。
十一月十四日早晨，他们到达目的地。菲利亚斯·福克一点时间也不肯浪费，当即登上“卡尔纳蒂克号”。从船上他得知，法国人万事通确实已在前一天乘这条船抵达。消息叫艾娥达欢喜极了。福克自己兴许也同样高兴，不过他的脸上仍不流露感情。

去旧金山的轮船据报就在当天晚上发船。因此，若能办到，非马上把万事通找到不可。福克先生向法、英两国领事求助，都没有结果。他沿街寻觅多时，找到失踪仆人的希望也开始变得渺茫。最后是机缘，或者说，是某种预感，把他领进了尊敬的巴图尔卡先生的剧场。万事通一身奇装异服，跟卖艺的人一个打扮，他肯定认不出；但仰面朝天的万事通偏从地上认出了楼座里的主人。他忍不住惊得动了一下，鼻子跟着移了位，整座“人塔”便乱做一团，轰然坍塌在舞台上。
这一连串事情，后来都是艾娥达亲口讲给万事通听的。她告诉他，从香港乘“坦卡代尔号”去上海途中发生了什么，同船还有一位名叫菲克斯的先生。
听见这个名字，万事通没有变脸。他觉得，现在还不是向主人揭露自己同警探之间那桩事的时候。至于他自己为什么会失踪，他只是解释说，自己在香港一间酒馆里喝醉了，又抽了鸦片，并为这件事道歉。
福克先生不动声色地听完，一言不发，随后给了仆人一笔钱，好让他买些跟自己身份相称的衣服。不到一个小时，法国人剪去了鼻子，脱去了翅膀，身上再找不出一点东西，让人想起那位天狗神的信徒。

这艘即将从横滨开往旧金山的轮船名叫“格兰特将军号”，属于太平洋邮船公司。它是一艘二千五百吨的大型明轮船，设备精良，速度极快。甲板上方，巨大的摇梁上下起伏，一端有活塞杆反复升降，另一端装着连杆，直接与桨轮轴相接，将直线运动转成圆周运动。“格兰特将军号”立有三根桅杆，可以张起大面积的风帆，大为增强蒸汽机的推动力。照每小时十二英里的航速，二十一天可以横渡太平洋。菲利亚斯·福克因此有充分理由希望，十二月二日到旧金山，十一日到纽约，二十日便可到伦敦。如此一来，离事关成败的十二月二十一日还可早出若干小时。

船上客满，有英国人，有许多美国人，有一大批前往加利福尼亚做工的劳工，又有几个驻东印度的军官，正利用假期环游世界。旅途中没有发生任何大事。仗着巨大的桨轮，这条船几乎不怎么摇晃，“太平洋”这三个字差不多名副其实。福克先生照旧沉静寡言。年轻的女伴却觉得，除了感恩之外，自己对他还有一层越来越深的眷恋。他沉默而慷慨的本性，比她自己意识到的更加打动她。她几乎不知不觉地任由这份感情滋长，它在那保护她的人身上，却仿佛没有引起半点反应。艾娥达把他的一切打算全放在心上，哪怕遇上一桩看来可能耽搁行程的事，也会为他焦急。

她常同万事通聊天，后者当然看得出这位女士的心事。他是最忠心不过的仆人，说到菲利亚斯·福克的诚实、慷慨和仗义，总说不尽赞美的话。艾娥达担心旅程难以顺利收场，他便费心劝慰她。他说，最困难的那一段已经过去；日本、中国那些令他眼花缭乱的地方已经留在后面，如今他们正向他心目中文明的国度去呢。从旧金山到纽约，坐一趟火车；从纽约到利物浦，再搭一艘横渡大西洋的轮船。这样，无疑便能在约定的期限内，完成这场看来不可能的环球之旅。

从横滨出发的第九天，按经度计算，菲利亚斯·福克已恰好绕过半个地球。十一月二十三日，“格兰特将军号”越过东经西经相交的一百八十度经线，正处在地球上经度与伦敦相对的地方。福克的八十天确实已用去五十二天，只剩二十八天。然而，照经度的差距，他只走了一半；若按实际路程，却已走过全程的三分之二。因为伦敦到亚丁、亚丁到孟买、加尔各答到新加坡、新加坡到横滨，每一段都非得绕一个大圈子不可。倘若能不偏不倚始终沿伦敦所在的北纬五十度纬线走，全程只有约一万二千英里。可是种种交通路线曲折不直，他实际非走二万六千英里不可。到了十一月二十三日，已经走完了一万七千五百英里。眼下总算是一条笔直的航程了，连菲克斯也已经不在跟前设置障碍了！
同样在十一月二十三日这天，万事通也有了一项欢喜的发现。你还记得，这个倔强的家伙坚持让那只大名鼎鼎的祖传银表永远走伦敦时间，一路经过的各地时间，他全认为不对，不可靠。可就在今天，他明明没拨过表针，却发现自己的表跟船上的精密钟丝毫不差。他得意得乐不可支，恨不得菲克斯就在船上，让他瞧瞧还有什么话说！
“那滑头跟我讲了一大堆鬼话，”万事通来来回回念叨，“什么子午线，什么太阳，什么月亮！月亮？我看是拿月光来糊弄人！听信这种人的话，钟点还能准到哪里去？我早知道，迟早有一天，太阳自己要拿我的表来对时！”

万事通并不知道，要是他那块表的表盘跟意大利的钟一样，分作二十四小时，他就没什么好得意的了。如今指针指着九点，他以为那是上午九点；若是二十四小时的表盘，就会标明是晚上九点，也就是从午夜算起的第二十一个钟头，这正是伦敦与一百八十度经线之间的时差。可就算菲克斯在场，能把这纯属物理的现象解释给他听，万事通即使听懂，也决不肯认。况且要是警探这会儿真在船上，万事通跟他要算的另有一桩事，动起手来的方式也会截然不同。
菲克斯此刻究竟在哪里？
其实，他就在“格兰特将军号”上。
一到横滨，菲克斯便同福克道别，心想当天晚些时候还会碰面，径直去了英国领事馆。他终于在那里找到了逮捕令。文件从孟买一路追在他身后，是有人以为他已经搭上了“卡尔纳蒂克号”，便让它跟那条船到了横滨。可想而知，意识到这张逮捕令现已无效时，菲克斯有多么失望。福克已经离开英国属地，眼下竟得走引渡的手续了！
“好吧，”生了一阵气，菲克斯暗自说道，“我的逮捕令在这里不作数，在英国可作数。看得出来，那坏蛋以为自己已把警察甩脱，打算回本国去。很好！我跟着他过大西洋。至于那笔钱，老天保佑，到时候可要剩下一点！可是路费、酬金、诉讼、交保、买象以及种种花费，他已经用去五千多英镑了。话又说回来，银行很有钱嘛！”
主意既定，他登上“格兰特将军号”。等福克先生和艾娥达上船时，他已经在了。最叫他大吃一惊的是，万事通尽管还穿着戏服，他却也把他认了出来。为免发生一场尴尬的解释，他赶紧藏进船舱，希望旅客这样多，福克先生的仆人不至于注意到他。
然而，偏在这一天，他在前甲板同万事通撞了个正着。万事通一言不发，一个箭步冲上来，扼住他的喉咙，朝警探结结实实来了一阵连珠炮似的拳头，把法国拳法比英国拳法高明多少好好表演了一回。一旁有几个美国人看得十分开心，立刻就开始往万事通身上下注。
万事通打完，只觉得神清气爽，心里舒服多了。菲克斯有些衣冠不整，站了起来，望着对手，冷冷地问：“打完了吗？”
“这一回——打完了。”
“那好，听我对你说句话。”
“事关你主人的利益。”
万事通仿佛被菲克斯的镇静压住了。他一声不响地跟在后面，两人避开别的旅客，找地方坐下。
“你打过我一顿了，”菲克斯说，“很好，我早料到有这回事。现在听我说。到目前为止，我一直站在福克先生的对面。从现在起，我要替他这一边出力。”
“啊哈！”万事通叫道，“您这下相信他是个正派人了？”
“不，”菲克斯冷冷地回答，“我认为他是个坏蛋。嘘，别动，听我把话说完。只要福克先生还在英国属地上，对我有利的办法，便是把他留在那里，直到逮捕令送到。我想尽一切手段拖他：让孟买的祭司去追他，在香港把你灌倒，使你和他分开，叫他误了去横滨的轮船。”
万事通捏紧了拳头，听着。
“现在呢，”菲克斯接着说，“看起来福克先生要回英国。很好，我跟他回英国去。可往后，从前我怎样费力把障碍摆到他路上，我就要怎样费力把障碍清开。瞧，我变了打法。道理也很简单：如今对我有利的，正是变一变打法。你的利益跟我的一致。唯有回到英国，你才能弄清，自己究竟侍候的是个罪犯，还是个正派人。”
万事通十分仔细地听了菲克斯的话，确信他说这些话确是出于真心。
“那么，我们是朋友了？”警探问。
“朋友？那算不上，”万事通回答，“不过也许可以算同盟。可是，只要有半点背信弃义的迹象，我就替您把脖子拧下来。”
“就这么定。”警探平平静静地说。
十一天以后，十二月三日，“格兰特将军号”驶进金门海峡的海湾，抵达旧金山。
福克先生既没有赢得一天，也没有亏掉一天。

sections.title_zh: 第25章　匆匆瞥见旧金山
sections.title_en: CHAPTER XXV. — IN WHICH A SLIGHT GLIMPSE IS HAD OF SAN FRANCISCO
source_paragraphs: It was seven in the morning when Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Passepartout set foot upon the American continent, if this name can be given to the floating quay upon which they disembarked. These quays, rising and falling with the tide, thus facilitate the loading and unloading of vessels. Alongside them were clippers of all sizes, steamers of all nationalities, and the steamboats, with several decks rising one above the other, which ply on the Sacramento and its tributaries. There were also heaped up the products of a commerce which extends to Mexico, Chili, Peru, Brazil, Europe, Asia, and all the Pacific islands.

Passepartout, in his joy on reaching at last the American continent, thought he would manifest it by executing a perilous vault in fine style; but, tumbling upon some worm-eaten planks, he fell through them. Put out of countenance by the manner in which he thus “set foot” upon the New World, he uttered a loud cry, which so frightened the innumerable cormorants and pelicans that are always perched upon these movable quays, that they flew noisily away.

Mr. Fogg, on reaching shore, proceeded to find out at what hour the first train left for New York, and learned that this was at six o’clock p.m.; he had, therefore, an entire day to spend in the Californian capital. Taking a carriage at a charge of three dollars, he and Aouda entered it, while Passepartout mounted the box beside the driver, and they set out for the International Hotel.

From his exalted position Passepartout observed with much curiosity the wide streets, the low, evenly ranged houses, the Anglo-Saxon Gothic churches, the great docks, the palatial wooden and brick warehouses, the numerous conveyances, omnibuses, horse-cars, and upon the side-walks, not only Americans and Europeans, but Chinese and Indians. Passepartout was surprised at all he saw. San Francisco was no longer the legendary city of 1849—a city of banditti, assassins, and incendiaries, who had flocked hither in crowds in pursuit of plunder; a paradise of outlaws, where they gambled with gold-dust, a revolver in one hand and a bowie-knife in the other: it was now a great commercial emporium.

The lofty tower of its City Hall overlooked the whole panorama of the streets and avenues, which cut each other at right-angles, and in the midst of which appeared pleasant, verdant squares, while beyond appeared the Chinese quarter, seemingly imported from the Celestial Empire in a toy-box. Sombreros and red shirts and plumed Indians were rarely to be seen; but there were silk hats and black coats everywhere worn by a multitude of nervously active, gentlemanly-looking men. Some of the streets—especially Montgomery Street, which is to San Francisco what Regent Street is to London, the Boulevard des Italiens to Paris, and Broadway to New York—were lined with splendid and spacious stores, which exposed in their windows the products of the entire world.
When Passepartout reached the International Hotel, it did not seem to him as if he had left England at all.

The ground floor of the hotel was occupied by a large bar, a sort of restaurant freely open to all passers-by, who might partake of dried beef, oyster soup, biscuits, and cheese, without taking out their purses. Payment was made only for the ale, porter, or sherry which was drunk. This seemed “very American” to Passepartout. The hotel refreshment-rooms were comfortable, and Mr. Fogg and Aouda, installing themselves at a table, were abundantly served on diminutive plates by negroes of darkest hue.

After breakfast, Mr. Fogg, accompanied by Aouda, started for the English consulate to have his passport _visaed_. As he was going out, he met Passepartout, who asked him if it would not be well, before taking the train, to purchase some dozens of Enfield rifles and Colt’s revolvers. He had been listening to stories of attacks upon the trains by the Sioux and Pawnees. Mr. Fogg thought it a useless precaution, but told him to do as he thought best, and went on to the consulate.

He had not proceeded two hundred steps, however, when, “by the greatest chance in the world,” he met Fix. The detective seemed wholly taken by surprise. What! Had Mr. Fogg and himself crossed the Pacific together, and not met on the steamer! At least Fix felt honoured to behold once more the gentleman to whom he owed so much, and, as his business recalled him to Europe, he should be delighted to continue the journey in such pleasant company.

Mr. Fogg replied that the honour would be his; and the detective—who was determined not to lose sight of him—begged permission to accompany them in their walk about San Francisco—a request which Mr. Fogg readily granted.

They soon found themselves in Montgomery Street, where a great crowd was collected; the side-walks, street, horsecar rails, the shop-doors, the windows of the houses, and even the roofs, were full of people. Men were going about carrying large posters, and flags and streamers were floating in the wind; while loud cries were heard on every hand.
“Hurrah for Camerfield!”
“Hurrah for Mandiboy!”
It was a political meeting; at least so Fix conjectured, who said to Mr. Fogg, “Perhaps we had better not mingle with the crowd. There may be danger in it.”
“Yes,” returned Mr. Fogg; “and blows, even if they are political, are still blows.”

Fix smiled at this remark; and, in order to be able to see without being jostled about, the party took up a position on the top of a flight of steps situated at the upper end of Montgomery Street. Opposite them, on the other side of the street, between a coal wharf and a petroleum warehouse, a large platform had been erected in the open air, towards which the current of the crowd seemed to be directed.

For what purpose was this meeting? What was the occasion of this excited assemblage? Phileas Fogg could not imagine. Was it to nominate some high official—a governor or member of Congress? It was not improbable, so agitated was the multitude before them.

Just at this moment there was an unusual stir in the human mass. All the hands were raised in the air. Some, tightly closed, seemed to disappear suddenly in the midst of the cries—an energetic way, no doubt, of casting a vote. The crowd swayed back, the banners and flags wavered, disappeared an instant, then reappeared in tatters. The undulations of the human surge reached the steps, while all the heads floundered on the surface like a sea agitated by a squall. Many of the black hats disappeared, and the greater part of the crowd seemed to have diminished in height.
“It is evidently a meeting,” said Fix, “and its object must be an exciting one. I should not wonder if it were about the ‘Alabama,’ despite the fact that that question is settled.”
“Perhaps,” replied Mr. Fogg, simply.
“At least, there are two champions in presence of each other, the Honourable Mr. Camerfield and the Honourable Mr. Mandiboy.”

Aouda, leaning upon Mr. Fogg’s arm, observed the tumultuous scene with surprise, while Fix asked a man near him what the cause of it all was. Before the man could reply, a fresh agitation arose; hurrahs and excited shouts were heard; the staffs of the banners began to be used as offensive weapons; and fists flew about in every direction. Thumps were exchanged from the tops of the carriages and omnibuses which had been blocked up in the crowd. Boots and shoes went whirling through the air, and Mr. Fogg thought he even heard the crack of revolvers mingling in the din, the rout approached the stairway, and flowed over the lower step. One of the parties had evidently been repulsed; but the mere lookers-on could not tell whether Mandiboy or Camerfield had gained the upper hand.

“It would be prudent for us to retire,” said Fix, who was anxious that Mr. Fogg should not receive any injury, at least until they got back to London. “If there is any question about England in all this, and we were recognised, I fear it would go hard with us.”
“An English subject—” began Mr. Fogg.
He did not finish his sentence; for a terrific hubbub now arose on the terrace behind the flight of steps where they stood, and there were frantic shouts of, “Hurrah for Mandiboy! Hip, hip, hurrah!”

It was a band of voters coming to the rescue of their allies, and taking the Camerfield forces in flank. Mr. Fogg, Aouda, and Fix found themselves between two fires; it was too late to escape. The torrent of men, armed with loaded canes and sticks, was irresistible. Phileas Fogg and Fix were roughly hustled in their attempts to protect their fair companion; the former, as cool as ever, tried to defend himself with the weapons which nature has placed at the end of every Englishman’s arm, but in vain. A big brawny fellow with a red beard, flushed face, and broad shoulders, who seemed to be the chief of the band, raised his clenched fist to strike Mr. Fogg, whom he would have given a crushing blow, had not Fix rushed in and received it in his stead. An enormous bruise immediately made its appearance under the detective’s silk hat, which was completely smashed in.
“Yankee!” exclaimed Mr. Fogg, darting a contemptuous look at the ruffian.
“Englishman!” returned the other. “We will meet again!”
“When you please.”
“What is your name?”
“Phileas Fogg. And yours?”
“Colonel Stamp Proctor.”

The human tide now swept by, after overturning Fix, who speedily got upon his feet again, though with tattered clothes. Happily, he was not seriously hurt. His travelling overcoat was divided into two unequal parts, and his trousers resembled those of certain Indians, which fit less compactly than they are easy to put on. Aouda had escaped unharmed, and Fix alone bore marks of the fray in his black and blue bruise.
“Thanks,” said Mr. Fogg to the detective, as soon as they were out of the crowd.
“No thanks are necessary,” replied Fix; “but let us go.”
“Where?”
“To a tailor’s.”

Such a visit was, indeed, opportune. The clothing of both Mr. Fogg and Fix was in rags, as if they had themselves been actively engaged in the contest between Camerfield and Mandiboy. An hour after, they were once more suitably attired, and with Aouda returned to the International Hotel.

Passepartout was waiting for his master, armed with half a dozen six-barrelled revolvers. When he perceived Fix, he knit his brows; but Aouda having, in a few words, told him of their adventure, his countenance resumed its placid expression. Fix evidently was no longer an enemy, but an ally; he was faithfully keeping his word.

Dinner over, the coach which was to convey the passengers and their luggage to the station drew up to the door. As he was getting in, Mr. Fogg said to Fix, “You have not seen this Colonel Proctor again?”
“No.”
“I will come back to America to find him,” said Phileas Fogg calmly. “It would not be right for an Englishman to permit himself to be treated in that way, without retaliating.”
